title: Cortez Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Cortez wells have a 40-foot median depth, but records range to 1,300 feet. See yields, costs, permits, and risks before buying.
h1: Cortez, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land near Cortez means looking past the well sticker price. DWR records within five miles show a median well depth of 40 feet, a median reported yield of 5.0 gallons per minute, and a median static water level of 15 feet. Those figures are useful for planning, but the local record also includes wells as deep as 1,300 feet and a wide range of reported production.

This page covers the permit history, likely drilling cost, water-level information, and the checks that matter before you buy or build in the Cortez area, including nearby Dolores, Lewis, and Towaoc.

sections.heading: Cortez wells are usually shallow, but not always
sections.html:
The 173 permits with reported total depth have a 40-foot median. The middle half runs from 29 to 100 feet, so a typical bid based on local records may be much shallower than a mountain or fractured-granite well. Still, the range is broad: the 90th percentile is 187 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 1,300 feet.

About 74% of wells are under 100 feet. Another 21% fall between 100 and 300 feet, while 3% are 300 to 600 feet and 2% exceed 600 feet. Local permits mostly identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with smaller numbers in the Mancos and Alluvial aquifers. A driller should review nearby logs, not price your lot from the median alone.

sections.heading: Reported yield is workable, but production varies
sections.html:
Only 12 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield statistics are less complete than the depth statistics. Among those reports, the median is 5.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 1.0 to 14.4 gallons per minute.

The spread matters for a buyer. Eight percent of reported wells produce under 1 gallon per minute, while 42% are in the 1-to-5 range. Twenty-five percent produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and another 25% report more than 15 gallons per minute. A low-producing well may still serve a household with storage, but confirm the well's permitted use, pump test, storage tank, and recovery before relying on it for a new home.

sections.heading: Cortez water levels look shallow in the limited records
sections.html:
Only 2 permits report a static water level, so there is not enough local water-level data to establish a dependable trend by decade. Those reported measurements have a median depth to water of 15 feet, with a middle half from 8 to 22 feet.

That shallow result can help a driller think about construction, casing, grout, and pump placement, but it should not be treated as a guarantee for an untested parcel. Water levels can vary with location, season, aquifer, pumping, and well construction. Ask for the actual static level and recovery information on any existing well, and have the driller compare logs from Cortez with properties toward Mancos, Towaoc, or Lewis.

sections.heading: Permit activity grew sharply in the newer records
sections.html:
The permit history shows one permit in the 1960s, 17 in the 1970s, 36 in the 1980s, 38 in the 1990s, 16 in the 2000s, 95 in the 2010s, and 48 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. Records include 331 permitted wells, with 148 marked as constructed.

Most listed wells are monitoring wells, at 53% of the use mix. Domestic or household wells account for 24%, stock wells 4%, and irrigation 1%. That distinction matters: a nearby permit does not automatically prove that a property has a domestic water supply. Confirm the permit number, permitted use, construction status, and any restrictions through Colorado DWR before closing.

The most active drillers in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 85 wells; Kilby'S Water Well Service, with 20; and Kenyon Drilling/Kenyon Motor, with 15. Those names show local record activity, not a recommendation.

sections.heading: A median-depth Cortez well pencils out differently from a finished system
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground around Cortez, the local drilling cost model uses a typical rate of $50 to $75 per foot. At the 40-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $2,000 to $3,000.

A usable water system costs more than the hole. Including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, the modeled finished-well cost is about $8,000 to $15,000 at the median depth. A deep outlier, difficult access, casing or grout requirements, low yield, or extra trenching can change the bid substantially. Get the driller to separate drilling, casing, development, pump equipment, electrical, and water testing in writing.

sections.heading: Cortez buyers should investigate water quality and site limits
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records within about ten miles include 19 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 9 historic mine features, and 10 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped sites do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to test existing or new well water and review the property's location before relying on it.

Low yield and dry holes are also real risks because reported production is limited to 12 wells and 8% of those reports are under 1 gallon per minute. Check septic setbacks, drainfield space, access for a drill rig, and the building location before purchasing. A well permit, a septic plan, and a buildable site need to work together.

sections.heading: What to do before buying land near Cortez
sections.html:
Start with the neighboring well records, but separate domestic wells from monitoring, stock, and irrigation permits. Compare total depth, aquifer description, static water level, reported yield, construction status, and permitted use. The nearby communities of Dolores, Lewis, Towaoc, and Mancos can provide useful comparison logs, but conditions can change across short distances.

For an existing home, obtain the permit, well construction record, pump information, water-quality testing, and a current flow or recovery evaluation. For vacant land, have a licensed driller assess access and the likely target before you set a house location. If the basin is over-appropriated, ask whether an augmentation plan or other water-supply requirement applies. Do not treat the median Cortez well as a promise for your parcel.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Cortez, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Cortez is 40 feet, and the middle half runs from 29 to 100 feet. About 74% of wells are under 100 feet. Conditions are not uniform: the 90th percentile is 187 feet, and the deepest record is 1,300 feet. Review neighboring logs before assuming a shallow well on your property.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Cortez?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $75 per foot in mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 40-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $2,000 to $3,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is modeled at about $8,000 to $15,000, before unusual site or construction conditions.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce near Cortez?
faq.a: Among the 12 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 5.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 1.0 to 14.4 gallons per minute. Eight percent report under 1 gallon per minute. Because yield reporting is limited, request the actual pump test, recovery information, storage capacity, and permitted use for the specific well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Cortez?
faq.a: A permit does not prove that well water is safe to drink. Records identify 19 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 9 historic mine features, and 10 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about ten miles. Test the specific well, especially before occupying a home, and review nearby environmental records with a qualified water professional.

faq.q: Are there many domestic wells near Cortez?
faq.a: The records contain 331 permitted wells, but the use mix is broader than household supply. Domestic or household wells make up 24%, while monitoring wells account for 53%; stock wells are 4% and irrigation wells are 1%. Confirm that a nearby permit is domestic, constructed, and authorized for the use you need before relying on it.
